Shiny apps using each visitor's Fabric access

Source: vignettes/shiny-integration.Rmd
shiny-integration.Rmd

fabricQueryR lets you build Shiny apps around data in Microsoft Fabric. You can use a regular Fabric connection with a shared account or the app’s own credentials; queries then use that connection’s permissions.

This vignette focuses on delegated access: each visitor signs in, and the Shiny helpers shown here use that user’s authorization for Fabric queries. The advantage is that the permissions you already manage in Fabric determine which data each user can access through the app. You can reuse those access rules without maintaining a second set in Shiny.

You can work with Warehouse and Lakehouse tables using SQL, semantic models using DAX, Eventhouse data using KQL, files and Delta tables in OneLake, or an API for GraphQL.

This guide starts with SQL: connect to a Warehouse or Lakehouse, run a query, and display the result in Shiny. It then shows how to build a dashboard from a semantic model using DAX, reusing the measures and relationships used by Power BI. The complete app includes both approaches and the other data sources, so you can see how each fits into a Shiny app.

Queries run in background R processes using Shiny’s ExtendedTask, keeping the app responsive while data loads. The shinyOAuth package handles Microsoft sign-in.

Setup

Install the packages

This integration currently requires the development versions of fabricQueryR and shinyOAuth. If you have both source checkouts, install shinyOAuth first:

devtools::install("../shinyoauth")
devtools::install(".")
install.packages(c("shiny", "bslib", "mirai", "promises", "DBI", "odbc"))

Use shiny 1.8.1 or later, bslib 0.7.0 or later, and promises 1.3.0 or later. The app uses mirai when installed. Without mirai, install future to use the future_promise() fallback. For SQL, install Microsoft ODBC Driver 18 for SQL Server separately on the computer running the app and its workers. DAX, KQL and GraphQL use HTTP APIs, so they do not need a database driver. OneLake’s additional dependencies are described under Other data sources below.

Arrange Microsoft sign-in

Your app needs a Web application registration in Microsoft Entra, the service that manages your organization’s Microsoft sign-in. Your Fabric or Microsoft 365 administrator can help set this up.

For SQL, add the Azure SQL Database delegated permission user_impersonation. A delegated permission allows the app to make requests using the signed-in person’s access. Users also need permission to connect to the database and read the requested data.

The registration needs a redirect URI: the address where Microsoft sends the visitor after sign-in. For local development, use http://localhost:8100/. The address in the registration and the app must match. A deployed app uses its public HTTPS address instead.

You will need the tenant ID, which identifies your organization’s directory; the client ID, which identifies your app; and a client secret, which the app uses during sign-in. Complete any administrator consent your organization requires before running the app.

Save the connection settings

The app reads settings with Sys.getenv(). For local development, put these in your user .Renviron file and restart R:

ENTRA_TENANT_ID=your-directory-id
ENTRA_CLIENT_ID=your-application-id
ENTRA_CLIENT_SECRET=your-client-secret
FABRIC_WAREHOUSE_SQL_SERVER=your-warehouse-sql-hostname
FABRIC_WAREHOUSE_SQL_DATABASE=your-warehouse-database

Copy the server and database names from your Warehouse’s SQL connection details. The Lakehouse section below gives the equivalent settings for its SQL analytics endpoint. Keep the client secret out of app code and version control; deployed apps can use the hosting service’s environment-variable or secret settings.

A complete example app

Save the following code as app.R in a new directory. Keep the entries you want in sources; to start with just a Warehouse, keep "Warehouse (SQL)" = "warehouse". The sign-in configuration automatically selects the services needed by those entries. If you keep other sources, add their settings and registration permissions as described below.

The SQL queries use an example dbo.Sales table; replace it with your own table. The other branches also use example table, column and measure names, described in their sections below.

library(shiny)
library(fabricQueryR)

use_mirai <- requireNamespace("mirai", quietly = TRUE)
if (use_mirai) {
  mirai::daemons(2)
  onStop(\() mirai::daemons(0), session = NULL)
} else {
  future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 2)
  onStop(\() future::plan(future::sequential), session = NULL)
}

# Keep the sources your app needs.
sources <- c(
  "Warehouse (SQL)" = "warehouse",
  "Lakehouse (SQL)" = "lakehouse",
  "Semantic model (DAX)" = "dax",
  "Eventhouse (KQL)" = "kql",
  "OneLake file" = "files",
  "OneLake Delta table" = "delta",
  "GraphQL API" = "graphql"
)
service_for <- c(
  warehouse = "sql",
  lakehouse = "sql",
  dax = "dax",
  kql = "kql",
  files = "onelake",
  delta = "onelake",
  graphql = "graphql"
)
config <- fabric_shiny_config(
  tenant_id = Sys.getenv("ENTRA_TENANT_ID"),
  client_id = Sys.getenv("ENTRA_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("ENTRA_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = Sys.getenv("ENTRA_REDIRECT_URI", "http://localhost:8100/"),
  services = unique(unname(service_for[sources]))
)

# Replace the example table, column and measure names with your own.
read_data <- function(source, token, year) {
  switch(
    source,
    warehouse = fabric_sql_query(
      server = Sys.getenv("FABRIC_WAREHOUSE_SQL_SERVER"),
      database = Sys.getenv("FABRIC_WAREHOUSE_SQL_DATABASE"),
      sql = "SELECT TOP (100) * FROM dbo.Sales",
      token = token,
      numeric_policy = "driver",
      verbose = FALSE
    ),
    lakehouse = fabric_sql_query(
      server = Sys.getenv("FABRIC_LAKEHOUSE_SQL_SERVER"),
      database = Sys.getenv("FABRIC_LAKEHOUSE_SQL_DATABASE"),
      sql = "SELECT TOP (100) * FROM dbo.Sales",
      token = token,
      numeric_policy = "driver",
      verbose = FALSE
    ),
    dax = {
      data <- fabric_pbi_dax_query(
        workspace_id = Sys.getenv("FABRIC_WORKSPACE_ID"),
        dataset_id = Sys.getenv("FABRIC_SEMANTIC_MODEL_ID"),
        dax = sprintf(
          r"(
          EVALUATE SUMMARIZECOLUMNS(
            'Product'[Category], TREATAS({%d}, 'Date'[Year]),
            "Sales", [Total Sales]
          )
        )",
          as.integer(year)
        ),
        token = token
      )
      if (ncol(data) == 2L) {
        names(data) <- c("Category", "Sales")
      }
      data
    },
    kql = fabric_kql_query(
      cluster = Sys.getenv("FABRIC_KQL_ENDPOINT"),
      database = Sys.getenv("FABRIC_KQL_DATABASE"),
      query = "Sales | take 100",
      token = token
    ),
    files = fabric_onelake_read_file(
      workspace = Sys.getenv("FABRIC_WORKSPACE_ID"),
      item = Sys.getenv("FABRIC_LAKEHOUSE_ID"),
      path = Sys.getenv("FABRIC_ONELAKE_FILE", "Files/sales.parquet"),
      token = token
    ),
    delta = fabric_onelake_read_delta_table(
      table_path = Sys.getenv("FABRIC_DELTA_TABLE", "Sales"),
      schema = Sys.getenv("FABRIC_DELTA_SCHEMA", "dbo"),
      workspace_name = Sys.getenv("FABRIC_WORKSPACE_ID"),
      lakehouse_name = Sys.getenv("FABRIC_LAKEHOUSE_ID"),
      limit = 100,
      token = token,
      verbose = FALSE
    ),
    graphql = {
      result <- fabric_graphql_query(
        api = Sys.getenv("FABRIC_GRAPHQL_ENDPOINT"),
        query = "query { sales(first: 100) { items { Category Amount } } }",
        error_policy = "error",
        token = token
      )
      do.call(rbind, lapply(result$data$sales$items, as.data.frame))
    }
  )
}

ui <- fabric_shiny_ui(
  fluidPage(
    titlePanel("Explore Fabric data"),
    actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
    actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),
    selectInput("source", "Data source", sources),
    conditionalPanel(
      "input.source === 'dax'",
      numericInput("year", "Year", 2026, min = 1900, max = 2100, step = 1)
    ),
    bslib::input_task_button("load", "Load data"),
    conditionalPanel("input.source === 'dax'", plotOutput("sales")),
    tableOutput("tables")
  ),
  "fabric",
  config
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  fabric <- fabric_shiny_server("fabric", config)
  query <- ExtendedTask$new(function(token, generation, source, year) {
    promises::then(token, function(token) {
      data <- if (use_mirai) {
        mirai::mirai(
          {
            library(fabricQueryR)
            read_data(source, token, year)
          },
          read_data = read_data,
          source = source,
          token = token,
          year = year
        )
      } else {
        promises::future_promise(read_data(source, token, year))
      }
      promises::then(data, function(data) {
        list(generation = generation, source = source, year = year, data = data)
      })
    })
  }) |>
    bslib::bind_task_button("load")

  observeEvent(input$login, fabric$login(), ignoreInit = TRUE)
  observeEvent(input$logout, fabric$logout(), ignoreInit = TRUE)
  observeEvent(
    input$load,
    {
      service <- service_for[[req(input$source)]]
      req(fabric$ready(service))
      query$invoke(
        fabric$access_token(service, async = TRUE),
        fabric$generation(),
        input$source,
        input$year
      )
    },
    ignoreInit = TRUE
  )

  result <- reactive({
    req(fabric$ready(service_for[[req(input$source)]]))
    value <- query$result()
    req(identical(value$generation, fabric$generation()))
    req(identical(value$source, input$source))
    if (input$source == "dax") {
      req(identical(value$year, input$year))
    }
    value$data
  })
  output$tables <- renderTable(head(result(), 100))
  output$sales <- renderPlot({
    req(input$source == "dax")
    data <- result()
    req(nrow(data) > 0)
    barplot(as.numeric(data$Sales), names.arg = data$Category, ylab = "Sales")
  })
}

shinyApp(
  ui,
  server,
  uiPattern = ".*",
  options = list(host = "127.0.0.1", port = 8100)
)

Run the directory with shiny::runApp("path/to/your/app"), then open http://localhost:8100/. Click Sign in, leave Warehouse (SQL) selected, and click Load data. The app displays up to 100 rows from your table. You can then adapt the query or choose another configured source.

SQL: Warehouse and Lakehouse

The two SQL entries use fabric_sql_query() with different endpoints. Both return an R table for renderTable(). The Warehouse uses the settings from Setup. To use the Lakehouse entry, copy the server and database names from its SQL analytics endpoint’s connection details:

FABRIC_LAKEHOUSE_SQL_SERVER=your-lakehouse-sql-hostname
FABRIC_LAKEHOUSE_SQL_DATABASE=your-lakehouse-database

Replace dbo.Sales with your table. For filters taken from Shiny inputs, use SQL parameters: for example, sql = "SELECT * FROM dbo.Sales WHERE Region = ?" with params = list(region). Pass region to the task as an ordinary value.

Both SQL branches use numeric_policy = "driver", which keeps the ODBC driver’s numeric representation. For exact numeric or Arrow results, see SQL queries and the ADBC backend.

DAX: a semantic-model dashboard

To use the semantic-model entry, add these settings to .Renviron and restart R:

FABRIC_WORKSPACE_ID=your-workspace-id
FABRIC_SEMANTIC_MODEL_ID=your-semantic-model-id

Use the semantic model’s ID, rather than a report’s ID. Add the Power BI Service delegated permission Dataset.Read.All to the registration. Each user needs Read and Build permission on the model, and the tenant must allow the Dataset Execute Queries REST API. See Microsoft’s DAX query requirements.

The example assumes 'Product'[Category], 'Date'[Year] and a [Total Sales] measure. Replace these with names from your model. Select Semantic model (DAX) in the app, choose a year present in the model, and click Load data to display the sales chart. Change the year and click Load data again to update it.

fabric_pbi_dax_query() sends DAX to an existing semantic model and returns an R table. In this example, SUMMARIZECOLUMNS() groups by product category, TREATAS() applies the selected year, and [Total Sales] is evaluated by the model. You can reuse business measures already defined there while designing the dashboard in Shiny.

The app renames the two returned columns to Category and Sales for use with renderTable() and renderPlot(). Replace the base R chart with ggplot2 or another Shiny output as needed. For a larger dashboard, use separate tasks for views that should load independently, or return one dataset that several outputs can share.

Requests run as the signed-in user; model permissions and any row-level security applicable to that user govern the result. The model remains the source of measures and relationships, while Shiny provides the dashboard UI.

How the background query works

The app uses three fabricQueryR functions to connect sign-in with your Shiny UI:

  • fabric_shiny_config() holds the sign-in settings and selects the services. Create it once, outside server().
  • fabric_shiny_ui() wraps your usual UI so the app can complete sign-in.
  • fabric_shiny_server() creates helpers for the current visitor. Call it inside server() so each visitor has their own connection.

The Load data button starts an ExtendedTask. First, fabric$access_token(service, async = TRUE) acquires the visitor’s token for the selected service. Then mirai runs read_data() in a background R process, or future_promise() does so if mirai is not installed. query$result() makes the result available to the Shiny outputs when it is ready. The task button stays busy until that work completes.

Read reactive inputs when calling $invoke(), before the worker starts. The example passes the source and year as ordinary values. It also passes fabric$generation(), which identifies the current sign-in. The result checks prevent data from an earlier sign-in or a different source or year being displayed. Signing out clears the outputs; an already running query can still finish. Signing in again requires a new click on Load data.

See Shiny’s nonblocking operations guide for more about ExtendedTask, and the mirai Shiny guide for its background workers. The mirai call explicitly supplies the reader function and query inputs, and loads fabricQueryR in the worker.

Other data sources

Each branch of read_data() uses a regular fabricQueryR function with the current user’s token. You can keep one branch, combine several sources in a dashboard, or replace the example queries. The displayed table shows at most 100 rows; the OneLake file branch reads the whole file before displaying it.

KQL: Eventhouse

Set the query URI and database from your KQL database’s connection details:

FABRIC_KQL_ENDPOINT=https://your-cluster.kusto.fabric.microsoft.com
FABRIC_KQL_DATABASE=your-kql-database

The app runs Sales | take 100 with fabric_kql_query(). Replace Sales with your table or use your own KQL query. The registration uses Azure Data Explorer’s delegated user_impersonation permission, and each user needs access to the database. See KQL queries for query parameters and results.

OneLake files and Delta tables

Set the workspace and Lakehouse IDs, together with the file or table to read:

FABRIC_WORKSPACE_ID=your-workspace-id
FABRIC_LAKEHOUSE_ID=your-lakehouse-id
FABRIC_ONELAKE_FILE=Files/sales.parquet
FABRIC_DELTA_TABLE=Sales
FABRIC_DELTA_SCHEMA=dbo

fabric_onelake_read_file() reads a Parquet, CSV or Arrow file into R. Install the arrow package for this branch. fabric_onelake_read_delta_table() reads a Delta table directly from OneLake, with limit = 100 in this example. Set the schema separately; use FABRIC_DELTA_SCHEMA= for a Lakehouse without schemas. The Delta reader needs reticulate and a compatible Python environment. fabric_delta_config(initialize = TRUE) prepares the runtime; see OneLake and Lakehouse for details.

These branches use Azure Storage’s delegated user_impersonation permission and the user’s OneLake access. SQL and direct Delta reads offer different ways to work with Lakehouse tables; choose the interface that suits your app.

GraphQL

Set the URL of an existing Fabric API for GraphQL:

FABRIC_GRAPHQL_ENDPOINT=https://your-api.graphql.fabric.microsoft.com/graphql

The example calls fabric_graphql_query() and turns the returned sales items into an R data frame. Replace the query and result$data$sales$items with the names in your API’s schema. error_policy = "error" reports a failed GraphQL query through the task’s output. Add the Power BI Service delegated permission GraphQLApi.Execute.All to the registration.

The API’s source connection determines access to the underlying data. To use each visitor’s source permissions, configure its single sign-on settings accordingly. See Microsoft’s GraphQL connection guidance and GraphQL queries.

Advanced configuration

Discovery and service permissions

The example uses known endpoints and IDs. Add "fabric" to services if you also want to discover workspaces and items. Its default permissions are Workspace.Read.All and Item.Read.All; you can choose a narrower set with scopes = list(fabric = "Item.Read.All") when using known item IDs.

A task that discovers an item and queries it needs a token for each service. For example, acquire both tokens in the Shiny process:

tokens <- promises::promise_all(
  fabric = fabric$access_token("fabric", async = TRUE),
  sql = fabric$access_token("sql", async = TRUE)
)

Resolve that promise before starting the background query, as the main app does for one token. With mirai, pass the resolved list as tokens = tokens. Inside the worker, create the item and query it:

warehouse <- fabric_item(
  workspace = Sys.getenv("FABRIC_WORKSPACE_ID"),
  item = Sys.getenv("FABRIC_WAREHOUSE_ID"),
  type = "Warehouse", token = tokens$fabric
)
data <- warehouse$sql_query(
  "SELECT TOP (100) * FROM dbo.Sales",
  token = tokens$sql, numeric_policy = "driver", verbose = FALSE
)

The package fills in full scope URLs, including SQL’s https://database.windows.net//user_impersonation. DAX and GraphQL share a Power BI token target; when both services are selected, their permissions are combined automatically. See Fabric REST scopes when choosing discovery permissions.

Sign-in also requests openid, profile and offline_access to identify the visitor and renew credentials. Identity comes from a validated ID token; Graph UserInfo and User.Read are not needed just to display the visitor’s name. The client secret authenticates the app during sign-in, while data requests use the visitor’s delegated access.

Using an existing shinyOAuth app

If your app already handles sign-in with shinyOAuth, its connection can supply a token to the same ExtendedTask. Declare the required token targets on the shinyOAuth client before sign-in. For a DAX target named power_bi, invoke the task with:

observeEvent(input$load, {
  connection <- req(auth$connection())
  query$invoke(
    connection$access_token(
      target = "power_bi",
      required_scopes = "https://analysis.windows.net/powerbi/api/Dataset.Read.All",
      min_valid_for = 60, async = TRUE
    ),
    connection$id, "dax", input$year
  )
}, ignoreInit = TRUE)

Adapt the result check to compare value$generation with the current auth$connection()$id, and keep the year check. For several managed authorizations, select one with auth$connection(selected_id) and follow shinyOAuth’s ownership and activity requirements. For synchronous calls in the Shiny process, fabric_shiny_token_provider() adapts an existing connection to the usual token argument.

Diagnosing connection problems

fabric$ready("dax") checks the permissions recorded for the connection. A query can still fail because of service settings, network problems or data permissions. Use fabric$status() to inspect connection state and fabric$prepare("dax") to retry preparing DAX access. A problem with one service can leave the others available. Use fabric$reauthorize() to start sign-in again.

For application error handling, shinyOAuth_access_error provides a context$reason field. interaction_required calls for explicit sign-in again; insufficient_scope calls for checking permissions and consent. refresh_pending means a synchronous call cannot yet get the renewed credential. SQL may wrap these errors in the parent of a fabric_sql_authentication_error.

Routine token refresh does not change generation() or rerun queries. A token passed to a worker is fixed for that invocation; it does not renew there. If it expires, start a new task to acquire a fresh token. Synchronous calls using a token provider retain fabricQueryR’s retry behavior: one HTTP 401 response can trigger token renewal and a request retry. prepare() and reauthorize() themselves do not replay data operations.

Connections and deployment

fabric_sql_query() opens and closes its own connection. If you use fabric_sql_connect() or $sql_connect() directly, close it with DBI::dbDisconnect(), usually through on.exit() in a helper function. Signing out does not close an already open DBI connection.

Set up the worker pool once when the app starts. The example uses two background R processes: mirai::daemons(2) when mirai is installed, or future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 2) otherwise. Adjust that count for your host. The workers serve all visitors, and onStop() shuts them down when the app stops. Return ordinary R data from a worker; keep live database connections and Arrow streams within the process that created them.

Use an exact registered HTTPS callback URL for deployment. The uiPattern = ".*" setting lets callback subpaths reach the app. Check your hosting service’s routing, reverse-proxy and cookie settings using shinyOAuth’s deployment guidance. The default local sign-in lifetime is eight hours; adjust reauth_after_seconds for your app. App logout does not sign the visitor out of Microsoft everywhere.

Standard Microsoft service hosts are allowed. A trusted gateway needs its exact hostname in endpoint_hosts, configured by the app author.
